implementation_notes: Swift has no buffer type, and value semantics mean a `struct` frame is copied on assignment, so the pair is written by hand behind an explicit owner (a class, or an `Atomic` holding a reference or optional). Swift 6's standard library provides `Synchronization.Atomic` (SE-0410, implemented in Swift 6.0) with `store`/`load`/`exchange` and explicit memory orderings: the writer finishes the next frame and publishes with `.releasing`, readers `load(ordering: .acquiring)` and get a complete snapshot. Before Swift 6 the `swift-atomics` package provided the same operations and remains the compatibility route. Rendering frameworks present their own frames, so the hand-written pair is mostly for simulation and game state.
pitfalls: `Atomic<Value>` requires the payload to be `AtomicRepresentable`: a frame with reference members is only atomically available as a reference (a class or an optional), and the struct's internals are never made atomic.
The orderings are load-bearing - `.relaxed` omits the release/acquire edge and lets readers see a published frame with unwritten contents.
`Mutex` (the companion primitive) is non-recursive: calling `withLock` from inside its own closure has platform-dependent behaviour, as the proposal warns.

variants.name: Synchronization.Mutex-guarded pair
variants.implementation_notes: When several fields or two buffers must move as one unit, wrap the pair in `Synchronization.Mutex` (SE-0433, implemented in Swift 6.0) and perform the swap inside `withLock` - the proposal's own example is `cache.withLock { $0[key] = resource }` - with readers taking the same lock to copy the current frame out. This is the simplest correct form when the swap is rare and the frame is a value type (copying out is cheap for small frames). The pre-Swift-6 equivalent is `Foundation.NSLock` (`lock()`/`unlock()` with `defer`).
pitfalls: `withLock`'s closure must not suspend or call back into the same mutex; the mutex is non-recursive and re-entry deadlocks.
Copying the frame out under the lock is O(size): keep it to value frames or hand out an immutable reference type instead.
On the older `NSLock` path a missing `defer { lock.unlock() }` on an early return wedges the buffer forever.
